title: What to automate first in a small business | 50agents
description: What to automate first: score each repeated task by how often, how long and what a mistake costs, then start with the frequent, low-risk ones.
h1: What to automate first in a small business
answer: Automate first the tasks you do every day or week that follow the same steps and are cheap to get wrong, such as logging payments, sorting email or sending yourself a summary.
Leave tasks that move money, commit you to something or decide about a person until last, and automate those with an approval step.

body.p: Write down every task you repeated last week. For each, fill in three numbers and multiply the first two.

body.p: High-risk tasks still benefit, just later and with a person approving each action. Most guides list jobs to automate; vcita’s list of first wins, for example, is scheduling and reminders, invoicing and payment follow-ups, client messages and simple marketing. Few say which to leave alone. A rule we use: anything that touches money, contracts or a relationship gets a human yes.

method.h2: How to start, step by step

steps.title: List last week’s repeated tasks
steps.body: From your calendar, sent mail and to-do list. Aim for 15.

steps.title: Score them
steps.body: Times a month times minutes each, and the cost of a mistake.

steps.title: Pick one Low-risk task from the top
Fix the process before automating it
steps.body: If the task is messy by hand (three places to look, steps in your head), tidy it first. Automating a broken process makes it break faster.

steps.title: Build it, check it for a week
steps.body: Look at every run. Then pick the next one.

wrong.title: Starting with the hardest task
wrong.body: The one you hate most is often the one with the most judgement. Win with a dull one first.

wrong.title: Automating a mess
wrong.body: The automation copies every inconsistency. Tidy the process by hand first.

wrong.title: Messages that sound like a robot
wrong.body: Clients notice. Keep anything customer-facing as a draft you approve.

wrong.title: Reminders to people who already paid
wrong.body: The automation did not know. Make sure it reads the latest status right before it sends.

wrong.title: Tool sprawl
wrong.body: Five tools for five automations. Prefer one place where you can see them all.

faqs.q: Where should a small business start with automation?
faqs.a: With a task done daily or weekly, the same way each time, where a mistake is cheap: logging orders or payments, sorting email, a weekly summary.
Anything that commits you (contracts, refunds, discounts) or decides about a person (hiring, firing) without a human approving it.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to start?
faqs.a: Most tools have a free tier or free credits enough to build and test one automation. See [how much automation costs](/guides/how-much-automation-costs-credits-tasks-and-runs-compared).

faqs.q: How do I know an automation is working?
faqs.a: Look at every run in its first week and compare it with what you would have done by hand. After that, check that it ran, not what it did, and read the runs again whenever something in the process changes.
